title: HTML Document Structure
description: Every HTML page follows a specific structure that browsers rely on to render content correctly.
content: An HTML document starts with the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration, which tells the browser this is an HTML5 document. The root <html> element contains two children: <head> for metadata and <body> for visible content. The <head> section includes the character encoding, viewport settings, and the page title. The <body> contains all the content users see — headings, paragraphs, images, links, and more. Understanding this structure is the foundation of all web development.
codeExample:
Hello, World!

This is my first web page.
keyPoints: <!DOCTYPE html> declares HTML5
<head> contains metadata, not visible content
<body> contains all visible page content
lang attribute helps screen readers and SEO

title: Semantic HTML Elements
description: Semantic elements convey meaning about the type of content they contain, improving accessibility and SEO.
content: Semantic HTML replaces generic <div> elements with meaningful tags like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, and <footer>. These elements communicate the structure of your page to browsers, screen readers, and search engines. A screen reader can jump directly to the <nav> element, and search engines understand that <article> contains self-contained content. Using semantic elements is not optional in professional development — it is a baseline requirement for accessibility compliance.
codeExample:
Home About Contact

Article Title

Article content goes here...

Related Links

© 2024 Epsilon Neote
keyPoints: <header> for introductory content or navigation
<main> for the dominant page content (only one per page)
<article> for self-contained content
<section> for thematic grouping with a heading
<aside> for tangentially related content
<footer> for footer information

title: HTML Forms & Inputs
description: Forms collect user input and are essential for search bars, login screens, registrations, and data entry.
content: The <form> element wraps all input controls. Each input should have a associated <label> for accessibility — use the for attribute on the label matching the id on the input. HTML5 provides many input types: text, email, password, number, date, checkbox, radio, range, color, file, and more. The required attribute enables browser-native validation. The <select> element creates dropdowns, and <textarea> handles multi-line input. Always set name attributes on inputs — they identify the data when the form is submitted.
codeExample:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
  <label for="name">Full Name</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

  <label for="lang">Language</label>
  <select id="lang" name="lang">
    <option value="js">JavaScript</option>
    <option value="py">Python</option>
    <option value="rb">Ruby</option>
  </select>

  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
keyPoints: Always pair <label> with inputs via for/id
HTML5 types like email and url provide free validation
required attribute prevents empty submissions
method attribute defines GET or POST
name attribute identifies data on the server side

title: The CSS Box Model
description: Every element on a page is a rectangular box governed by the box model — content, padding, border, margin.
content: The box model defines how space is calculated for every element. Content is the innermost area holding text or children. Padding adds space between content and the border. Border wraps the padding. Margin creates space between this element and neighbors. By default, width and height set the content dimensions, meaning padding and border increase the total size. Using box-sizing: border-box changes this so width and height include padding and border — this is almost always what you want. Most resets apply border-box globally.
keyPoints: box-sizing: border-box is the modern default
margin collapses vertically between siblings
padding does NOT collapse
auto margins center block elements horizontally
outline does not take up space (unlike border)

title: Flexbox Layout
description: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system for arranging items in rows or columns with powerful alignment controls.
content: Set display: flex on a container to activate flexbox. The main axis defaults to row (horizontal). Use justify-content to align items along the main axis and align-items for the cross axis. flex-direction: column flips the axes. The gap property adds space between flex children without margin hacks. Children can use flex: 1 to grow equally, or flex-grow, flex-shrink, and flex-basis for fine control. Flexbox handles vertical centering trivially — align-items: center on the container. It also reorders items visually with the order property without changing DOM structure.
keyPoints: display: flex activates flexbox on the container
justify-content aligns on the main axis
align-items aligns on the cross axis
gap replaces margin-based spacing between items
flex: 1 makes items grow equally to fill space
flex-wrap: wrap allows items to flow to new lines

title: CSS Grid Layout
description: Grid is a two-dimensional layout system for creating complex page layouts with rows and columns simultaneously.
content: Set display: grid on a container. Define columns with grid-template-columns and rows with grid-template-rows. The fr unit distributes fractional space — 1fr 2fr gives one column a third of the space and another two-thirds. repeat(3, 1fr) creates three equal columns. Use grid-column and grid-row on children to span multiple cells. grid-area with grid-template-areas lets you name regions for intuitive layout definitions. Grid excels at page-level layouts while flexbox handles component-level alignment. They work perfectly together.
keyPoints: grid-template-areas enables named layout regions
fr unit distributes available space fractionally
repeat() function avoids repetitive column/row definitions
minmax() sets flexible size ranges for responsive grids
gap applies to both rows and columns
Grid and Flexbox complement each other — use both

title: Variables & Data Types
description: JavaScript has three variable declarations and seven primitive types, plus objects and arrays.
content: Use const by default, let when you need reassignment, and never use var. const prevents reassignment but does NOT make objects immutable — you can still modify properties. let is block-scoped, var is function-scoped (and hoisted), which causes bugs. Primitive types are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, and symbol. Objects and arrays are reference types — variables hold a reference to the data, not the data itself. This means two variables can point to the same object, and modifying one affects the other.
keyPoints: Use const by default, let only when reassignment is needed
Avoid var — it is function-scoped and hoisted
Primitives are copied by value, objects by reference
typeof null returns 'object' — a historical bug
Use typeof to check types at runtime

title: Functions & Closures
description: Functions are first-class citizens in JS. Closures allow inner functions to access outer scope even after the outer function returns.
content: JavaScript supports function declarations, function expressions, and arrow functions. Arrow functions do not have their own this binding — they inherit this from the enclosing scope. A closure is created when a function references variables from its outer lexical scope. Even after the outer function returns, the inner function retains access to those variables. Closures enable data privacy, factory functions, and the module pattern. They are also why callbacks in event handlers and setTimeout can access variables defined in their surrounding scope.
keyPoints: Arrow functions inherit this from the enclosing scope
Closures retain access to outer scope after the outer function returns
Closures enable private state and encapsulation
Functions can be passed as arguments and returned from other functions
IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) creates a private scope

title: Async JavaScript
description: Handle asynchronous operations with Promises and async/await — network requests, timers, and file operations.
content: JavaScript is single-threaded but non-blocking, thanks to the event loop. Promises represent a value that will be available in the future — either resolved (success) or rejected (error). The async keyword makes a function return a Promise, and await pauses execution until a Promise settles. Always wrap await in try/catch for error handling. Promise.all runs multiple promises in parallel and resolves when all succeed. Promise.allSettled resolves when all settle regardless of outcome. Promise.race resolves with the first promise to settle.
keyPoints: async functions always return a Promise
await can only be used inside async functions
Always handle errors with try/catch around await
Promise.all runs promises in parallel
The event loop enables non-blocking I/O in a single thread

title: Python Basics & Syntax
description: Python uses indentation for block structure, dynamic typing, and a clean readable syntax.
content: Python uses indentation (4 spaces) instead of braces to define code blocks. Variables are dynamically typed — Python infers the type at runtime. Use snake_case for variables and functions, PascalCase for classes. Strings support f-strings for formatting: f'Hello {name}'. Lists are mutable sequences, tuples are immutable, dictionaries are key-value maps, and sets store unique elements. The range() function generates number sequences. Python's philosophy emphasizes readability — there should be one obvious way to do something.
codeExample:
# Variables — no type declaration needed
name = "Epsilon"
version = 3.12
is_active = True

# F-strings for formatting
message = f"Welcome to {name} v{version}"

# List operations
skills = ["HTML", "CSS", "JS"]
skills.append("Python")
first = skills[0]    # "HTML"
sliced = skills[1:]  # ["CSS", "JS", "Python"]

# Dictionary
config = {
    "theme": "dark",
    "language": "en",
    "debug": False,
}

# Comprehensions
upper_skills = [s.upper() for s in skills]
even = [x for x in range(20) if x % 2 == 0]
keyPoints: Indentation defines code blocks — 4 spaces is standard
Dynamic typing — no variable type declarations
F-strings are the preferred string formatting method
Lists are mutable, tuples are immutable
List comprehensions replace many map/filter patterns

title: Functions & Decorators
description: Python functions are first-class objects. Decorators modify function behavior without changing source code.
content: Functions in Python are objects — they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions. Default arguments are evaluated once at function definition, so mutable defaults like [] cause bugs — use None instead. *args collects positional arguments into a tuple, **kwargs collects keyword arguments into a dict. Decorators wrap a function to add behavior — logging, timing, access control, caching. The @syntax is syntactic sugar for applying the decorator. functools.wraps preserves the original function's metadata.
codeExample:
import functools
import time

# Decorator that times function execution
def timer(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
        print(f"{func.__name__} took {elapsed:.4f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper

@timer
def process_data(items):
    return [x ** 2 for x in items]

result = process_data(range(10000))
# Output: process_data took 0.0012s

# Mutable default argument pitfall
def add_item(item, items=None):  # NOT items=[]
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items
keyPoints: Functions are first-class objects in Python
Mutable default arguments are a common bug — use None
*args and **kwargs handle variable arguments
Decorators add behavior without modifying function source
@functools.wraps preserves function metadata in decorators

title: Components & JSX
description: React UIs are built from reusable components. JSX is a syntax extension that looks like HTML in JavaScript.
content: React components are functions that return JSX — a syntax that resembles HTML but compiles to JavaScript. Component names must start with an uppercase letter. JSX uses className instead of class, htmlFor instead of for, and camelCase for event handlers like onClick. Expressions go inside curly braces: {variable}. Components accept props (inputs) and render output based on them. Props are read-only — a component should never modify its own props. Fragment (<></>) groups elements without adding DOM nodes.
keyPoints: Component names must start with uppercase
Use className instead of class in JSX
Curly braces {} embed JavaScript expressions in JSX
Props are read-only inputs to components
Fragments (<></>) avoid unnecessary wrapper divs

title: Hooks: useState & useEffect
description: Hooks let functional components manage state and side effects — the two core concerns of any interactive UI.
content: useState returns a state variable and a setter function. The setter can accept a new value or an updater function that receives the previous state — always use the updater form when the new state depends on the old. useEffect runs side effects after render: data fetching, subscriptions, DOM manipulation. The dependency array controls when the effect re-runs — empty [] runs once on mount, [dep] runs when dep changes, and no array runs every render. Return a cleanup function from useEffect to tear down subscriptions and timers. Never call hooks conditionally — they must run in the same order every render.
keyPoints: useState returns [value, setter] — use updater form for derived state
useEffect runs after render — dependency array controls re-runs
Return cleanup function from useEffect for subscriptions/timers
Never call hooks inside conditions or loops
Use a cancelled flag to prevent state updates after unmount

title: Context & Custom Hooks
description: Context provides shared state across the component tree. Custom hooks extract reusable logic.
content: React Context avoids prop drilling — passing props through many intermediate components. Create context with createContext(), provide it with <Context.Provider value={...}>, and consume it with useContext(). Context is best for theme, locale, auth, and other app-wide data. For complex state with many actions, useReducer centralizes state transitions. Custom hooks extract stateful logic into reusable functions — name them starting with use. A useLocalStorage hook that syncs state to localStorage, a useFetch hook that manages loading/error/data — these patterns dramatically reduce duplication.
keyPoints: Context avoids prop drilling for app-wide data
Provider wraps the tree, useContext consumes it
useReducer centralizes complex state transitions
Custom hooks extract reusable stateful logic
Custom hook names must start with 'use'
